title: Peregrin and the Gentle Ogre
markdown:
Peregrin the young wizard lived on the dark pine-covered slopes of Owlglass Mountain. His home was a cozy cottage. It smelled a little like rosemary and, sometimes, a sweet, slightly burnt sugar smell that magic left behind. Sunlight, when it managed to peek through the dense pine branches, painted patterns of light and dark on his worn wooden floor. His best friend, and most of the time, his only companion, was Scruffy, a lizard whose scales shimmered like lots of tiny emeralds. Scruffy wasn't just any lizard; he was Peregrin’s pet, and a rather sleepy one at that. He had a talent for finding the warmest, most comfortable spots, which often happened to be Peregrin’s shoulder, or even, on particularly chilly days, the pocket of his robe.

One crisp morning, the market bell chimed in the distance, a sound that usually made Peregrin’s heart do a little flip of excitement. But today, it made him frown. Oh dear, a mess! He’d promised Mrs. Higgins the rare Moonpetal bloom for her special honey cakes. The Moonpetals were very hard to find. They only bloomed under soft moonlight, and their petals had a shine that reminded Peregrin of starlight. Unfortunately, in his haste yesterday, he’d accidentally traded the last precious Moonpetal for a rather nice, even though it wobbled a bit, walking stick that looked so much like a badger. He’d been so charmed by its twitching wooden nose! Mrs. Higgins was expecting it! The market would be buzzing with folk soon, and Peregrin needed to fix this silly mistake before the first stall even opened its shutters.

“Come on, Scruffy,” Peregrin called, adjusting his pointy hat which had a habit of tipping over. “We need to find another Moonpetal. And try to stay awake this time, please! I have a feeling we might need your keen eyes… or at least, not your napping abilities.”

Scruffy blinked his golden eyes, which were the colour of warm honey, and gave a little flick of his tail. He scuttled onto Peregrin’s shoulder, settling into a warm, familiar spot right by Peregrin’s ear. He let out a tiny, contented sigh, which sounded remarkably like a small gust of wind.

They ventured into the whispering pine woods that climbed the gentle slopes of Owlglass Mountain. The air was cool and carried the fresh pine smell, mingled with the damp, earthy aroma of the forest floor. Sunlight dappled through the thick canopy overhead, creating patterns of light and dark on the mossy ground. Peregrin hummed a little tune, a jaunty melody about brave knights and mischievous sprites, as he searched for the silvery glow of a Moonpetal. He looked under broad, velvety fern leaves and behind old tree roots that twisted like fingers.

“Here, Scruffy,” Peregrin whispered, pointing to a patch of particularly deep, emerald-green moss. “Do you see it? The Moonpetal should be right… oh.”

Scruffy, who had been perched on Peregrin’s outstretched finger, his tiny claws tickling Peregrin’s skin, was now fast asleep. His little emerald body was curled up in a ball, his head resting on his tail. His tiny snores were barely audible, a soft, rustling sound like leaves skittering across the ground. It was quite the talent, really, falling asleep so suddenly.

“Oh, Scruffy,” Peregrin sighed, a fond smile tugging at his lips. He carefully scooped up the sleeping lizard and tucked him into his cloak pocket, making sure he was snug and wouldn't tumble out. “Well, I suppose it’s just me then. Just me and my own two eyes, and perhaps a slightly worried feeling in my tummy.”

Peregrin continued his search, his brow furrowed in concentration. He walked deeper into the woods, where the trees grew closer together, their branches weaving together like a protective ceiling, and the shadows danced with a playful mystery. Suddenly, he heard a soft, muffled sound, like a giant sigh that had been caught in a particularly thick cloud. It was a sound full of sadness.

He peered through thick, hanging ivy and saw a truly huge creature sitting with his knees pulled up to his chest. It was an ogre, a very big creature, and by the looks of him, very gloomy. But unlike the roaring, stomping ogres from tales told by the firelight, this one looked… sad. He had big, gentle eyes, the colour of deep pools, that seemed to be watching a ladybug meticulously crawling up a blade of grass. He seemed entirely absorbed in its tiny, determined journey.

“Hello?” Peregrin said, his voice a little shaky, though he tried to make it sound brave.

The ogre jumped, a sound like a small landslide of pebbles. He quickly tried to hide his face behind his massive, tree-trunk-like hands. “Oh dear,” he rumbled, his voice deep and a little shaky, like distant thunder. “Please don’t be cross. I didn’t mean to be so big. It just… happens.”

Peregrin, though a little surprised by the sheer size of the creature, didn’t feel scared. The ogre’s voice was so gentle, and his eyes looked so worried, like a lost puppy’s. “I’m not cross at all,” Peregrin said kindly, taking a step closer. “I’m Peregrin. Are you alright? You look… rather thoughtful.”

The ogre peeked through his enormous fingers. “I’m… I’m Grumbles,” he whispered, his voice barely louder than a soft breeze. “Everyone runs away. They think I’m going to stomp or roar or… or eat their hats. But I just like watching ladybugs.” He pointed a huge, thick finger, calloused like old bark, at the tiny red creature. “She’s very determined, isn’t she? I admire her spirit.”

Peregrin chuckled, the sound light and clear in the quiet woods. “She certainly is. I’m looking for a Moonpetal bloom, have you seen any around here?”

Grumbles’s eyes widened, and a flicker of something hopeful crossed his face. “A Moonpetal? Oh! They grow near my favorite quiet spot, by the gurgling brook. I always leave them be. They’re too pretty to pick, don't you think? They look like little fallen stars.” He stood up slowly, a movement that made the ground shake just a little, like a gentle earthquake. “I can show you. If you’re not afraid of… well, of me.”

“Not at all,” Peregrin assured him. He gently pulled Scruffy from his pocket. The lizard was just waking up, blinking sleepily and stretching his little emerald limbs. “Scruffy, meet Grumbles. Grumbles, meet Scruffy. He’s not very talkative before his second nap, which is usually around elevenses.”

Grumbles’s large, somewhat rugged face cracked into a shy smile, revealing surprisingly few, but rather large, teeth. “He’s… he’s a very small creature. Like a jewel, he is. A very sleepy jewel.”

Together, Peregrin and Grumbles walked towards the brook. Grumbles moved with surprising grace for someone so large, his enormous feet treading with remarkable care, like a dancer trying not to crush invisible flowers. He carefully stepped over roots and around small bushes, his large hands occasionally reaching out to steady himself against a tree trunk, leaving no mark. He pointed with his enormous finger, stained with faint colours from where he’d been painting pebbles. “Just beyond those mossy rocks. You’ll see them.”

And there they were! A small patch of Moonpetals, their silvery petals unfurling in the dappled light, catching the sunbeams and reflecting them back with a soft, magical glow. They shimmered with a soft light, truly like captured moonlight. Peregrin gasped, his eyes wide with wonder.

“Oh, thank you, Grumbles!” Peregrin exclaimed, his voice full of genuine delight. He carefully picked one, its stem cool and slender in his hand. “Mrs. Higgins will be so pleased. And I shall have to remember to thank you properly, not just for the flower, but for… well, for being you.”

“You’re welcome, Peregrin,” Grumbles rumbled, his smile reaching his kind eyes, making them crinkle at the corners. “It’s nice to help someone who isn’t afraid of me. It’s a rather rare and pleasant experience.”

Peregrin looked at Grumbles, truly looked at him, and understood. Grumbles wasn't scary; he was just lonely. His size was a barrier, and his shyness made it worse. “You know,” Peregrin said, a new idea popping into his head, much like the Moonpetal in his hand, “the market is opening soon. If you come with me, perhaps people will see how kind you are. And maybe… maybe you could have a stall selling your beautiful painted stones? I’ve seen them before, tucked away by the roadside – they’re absolutely marvelous! Each one is like a tiny, colourful world.”

Grumbles looked down at his large hands, turning them over as if seeing them for the first time. Then he looked back at Peregrin, a flicker of hesitant hope dancing in his deep-set eyes. “Really? They wouldn’t… they wouldn’t run away screaming? Or throw rotten apples?”

“Not if you’re with me,” Peregrin promised, his voice firm and reassuring. He gently placed Scruffy back on his shoulder. Scruffy, now fully awake and observing the world with his usual calm demeanor, seemed to nod approvingly, his little head bobbing a couple of times.

As they approached the bustling market, Peregrin walked with confident purpose beside Grumbles, holding the precious Moonpetal bloom for Mrs. Higgins. He introduced Grumbles to everyone he met, explaining how the gentle ogre had helped him find the rare flower. The folk at the market, accustomed to Peregrin’s friendly ways and seeing his genuine trust in the huge creature, began to relax. They saw Grumbles's shy smiles and his careful, deliberate movements. And then they saw his stunning painted stones, each one a miniature masterpiece of swirling colours and delightful patterns. By the time the market bell rang its final, echoing chime, Grumbles had made several sales and, more importantly, several new friends. Peregrin, having solved his misunderstanding with Mrs. Higgins and made a most unexpected and wonderful new friend, felt a warmth spread through him that was even better than a bubbling cauldron of potent magic. And Scruffy, nestled on his shoulder, let out a soft, contented sigh, his third nap of the day successfully, and quite happily, avoided.
